title: The Secret Terms of Trump’s Venezuelan Oil Deal
author: Sebastian Rotella
content:
In late August, President Donald Trump announced what he called the “biggest
oil deal in world history.” Since then, the full text of the accord — which
grants the U.S. sweeping access to Venezuela’s oil reserves — has been one of
the most sought-after secrets in Washington, D.C.

ProPublica has reviewed a copy of the 18-page strategic partnership agreement
signed for the United States by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense
Secretary Pete Hegseth. The document reveals carefully constructed terms that
favor U.S. interests at every turn and cements the power of a small group of
people handpicked by the Trump administration to govern and profit from the
deal. The role of the Venezuelan government and the potential benefits to its
people are largely absent from the text.

One of the most criticized aspects of Trump’s announcement has been his choice
of a partner: Alejandro Betancourt, a globe-trotting Venezuelan oligarch who
has faced money-laundering investigations in three countries.

The Trump administration is taking a 35% stake in Betancourt’s firm, North
American Blue Energy Partners, by acquiring shares in a Barbados-registered
parent company. The deal document provides little information about the owners
and investors behind the parent company, who could receive enormous wealth
from the arrangement.

The agreement also safeguards Betancourt’s position as chief executive of
NABEP and says the U.S. government will work with the parent company to
appoint a powerful seven-member board to govern the venture for an initial
15-year term. Those aspects of the deal, according to people with knowledge of
how it came together, were designed to prevent future U.S. and Venezuelan
leaders from dismantling the enterprise.

Orlando Alvarado, a name not disclosed by the Trump administration as a party
to the accord, signed the agreement on behalf of the parent company, alongside
Betancourt, Hegseth and Rubio. Alvarado has held senior roles in multiple
Betancourt businesses, including as chief financial officer of an energy firm
that became embroiled in scandals a decade ago. According to [the Miami
Herald](https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/article236793383.html), federal
prosecutors identified Alvarado as an unindicted co-conspirator in a scheme to
embezzle money from Venezuela’s national oil company.

NABEP spokesperson Terry Wade said that “neither Mr. Betancourt nor Mr.
Alvarado has ever been charged with any crime in any country, and any claims
against them are baseless.”

* * *

### Do You Know More About This Topic?

We’re still reporting. If you know more about this topic, please contact our
reporting team.

**Cate Brown**

I’m interested in talking to people who understand how members of the Trump
administration, or their family members, are doing business, at home or
abroad.

[Contact Me](https://www.propublica.org/people/cate-brown)

* * *

Key aspects of the plan differ from the Trump administration’s public
pronouncements. Trump has said the deal will secure America’s energy dominance
for the next century. But the text indicates that U.S. purchasing rights
expire in half that time and that the underlying operating rights [appear to
run afoul](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/26/donald-trump-oil-
deal-with-venezuela) of [Venezuelan
laws](http://www.gacetaoficial.gob.ve/storage/2026/6978-2026-01-29-EXTRAORDINARIA.pdf)
limiting oil concessions to 25 years.

The agreement does ensure the United States a deep discount from fair-market
value on 20% of NABEP’s oil, as Trump has said. It does not, however,
explicitly guarantee that Betancourt’s company is obligated to pay the
estimated $200 billion in royalties and tax payments to Venezuela that [the
White House has said would benefit the
country](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/08/fact-sheet-president-
donald-j-trump-announces-historic-oil-agreement-to-secure-american-energy-
dominance-and-drive-venezuelas-economic-recovery/).

There are also significant caveats related to Trump’s central selling point to
Americans — that the deal will bring a gusher of low-cost oil imports.

The agreement gives the U.S. the right to purchase 20% of NABEP’s oil at a
discounted rate of $30 a barrel, or less than a third of what oil has sold for
in recent months, according to one of three supporting documents reviewed by
ProPublica.

But this fee does not account for the cost of getting Venezuela’s oil out of
the country. Much of Venezuela’s raw crude is so thick that it won’t flow
through pipelines unless it is first blended with 20% or more of oil thinner
products. Under the deal, the potentially significant cost of importing
millions of barrels of those blending materials is not included in the price.

The White House, the State Department, the Pentagon and the energy company
NABEP all defended the agreement, saying in statements that their new public-
private venture will provide meaningful and lasting economic benefits to both
countries that cannot be captured in a legal document.

“This historic deal marks a major step toward stabilizing Venezuela’s economy
after years of hyperinflation and almost no new investment, while more than
doubling the United States’ oil reserves,” said White House spokesperson
Taylor Rogers.

Wade emphasized that NABEP was chosen because of its track record of expanding
oil production in Venezuela in recent years and that the agreement was between
the company and the U.S. government, not Venezuela.

“Thanks in large part to the agreement,” Wade said, “there is a surge in
confidence about the future of Venezuela's oil industry and, as a direct
result, substantial new investments are flowing into the country.”

He added that much of NABEP’s oil comes from fields that require little or no
blending materials and that blending costs would not meaningfully impact the
price of production. “Our barrel economics are strong.”  

The newly revealed details of the agreement are nonetheless likely to raise
more questions about whether the unorthodox marriage of the United States and
a foreign energy baron can bring lasting benefits to either country — and
which private parties might benefit along the way. Trump’s oil deal is likely
to face scrutiny in both the United States and Venezuela, especially if
Democrats win one or both chambers in the midterm elections, according to
former U.S. diplomats and congressional staff.

“Question number one in a new U.S. Congress will be: Why Betancourt?” said
former Ambassador James Story, who served as the top U.S. diplomat in Caracas
from 2018 to 2023, in an interview. “Why did he get this deal? And was he
involved in criminality? It seems reasonable to have a congressional hearing
about those questions.”

> “Question number one in a new U.S. Congress will be: Why Betancourt?”
>
> James Story, former U.S. ambassador to Venezuela

In public comments, Delcy Rodríguez, who won the backing of the Trump
administration to serve as Venezuela’s interim president, [praised the accord
as “historic.”](https://www.facebook.com/dw.espanol/videos/delcy-
rodr%C3%ADguez-defiende-el-acuerdo-petrolero-con-ee-uula-presidenta-
encargada-d/1080128337799196/) She has asserted that Venezuela will retain
sovereignty over its natural resources and defended the choice of Betancourt.

People with knowledge of the Trump administration’s behind-the-scenes
decision-making and negotiations with Betancourt spoke to ProPublica on
condition of anonymity because they were either not authorized to do so or
were fearful of retribution.

One reason that the precise terms of the deal have remained hidden until now
is that the signed agreement is marked as a “sensitive” government document.
That classification is commonly used to shield a variety of federal records
from public release, including those containing personnel information, details
about ongoing law enforcement operations and matters protected by attorney-
client privilege. The document also contains a confidentiality clause barring
Betancourt’s company from disclosing the “existence and terms” of the U.S.
government agreement.

One person familiar with the deliberations said that people close to the Trump
administration  seemed keen to partner with Betancourt’s company because of
the privacy and flexibility it offered. That appeared to give NABEP an
advantage over publicly traded oil companies, which would be obligated to
shareholder reporting requirements.

“For example,” the person said, “Chevron couldn’t give 35% of their shares to
the Pentagon.”

A man in a suit sits to her right, and a woman in a suit sits to her left. She
is flanked by two Venezuelan flags. The three of them look toward TV cameras
off to one side. The room is lavishly decorated, with a chandelier, long
golden curtains over the doorways and a large framed painting of a person

interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, center, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris

Presidential Palace in Caracas in September. Juan Barreto/AFP via Getty Images

### The Deal

The oil deal is sensitive partly because of likely resistance in Venezuela,
where critics have already described it as a U.S. takeover of the country’s
precious natural resources.

A ProPublica analysis shows that its terms favor American interests at nearly
every turn and try to enshrine**** the Trump administration’s imprint
indefinitely.

The document states that a majority of the seven-member board must be U.S.
citizens at all times, and the U.S. government can appoint one “non-voting
observer” to join the group. Betancourt, who will serve as the chief
executive, is the only board member named by the agreement. The initial board
will establish the process for choosing new members.

“Throughout the evolution of the deal, it was clear that the governing
structure was intended to ensure maximum control by the people making the deal
and to insulate them from future administrations seeking to reverse the
agreement or call it into question,” a person familiar with the negotiations
said.

There is no requirement for any Venezuelan government participation in the
board.

The agreement also offers long-lasting protections for Betancourt and unnamed
investors. It requires a supermajority vote of five to oust Betancourt as CEO,
change the board composition or execute any transactions with a shareholder
that isn’t the U.S. government, an indirect equity holder, director, affiliate
or “immediate family members.”

The board will determine compensation for Betancourt in his role as chief
executive, the document says. As structured, the deal does not appear to
require any public disclosures about pay or distribution of shares to
executives.

The agreement does not say which shareholders, affiliates or family members
have been approved to transact with Betancourt’s company. Under Barbados
corporate law, there is almost nothing that can force those interests to be
revealed publicly.

The agreement does, however, require the company to maintain “anti-money
laundering controls,” submit to external audits and inspections of its records
by the U.S. government, and provide the U.S. government with an annual budget
and quarterly unaudited financial statements. It is unclear if these reports
will ever be made public.

It could be some time before the company produces enough oil to fulfill a
significant share of U.S. demand. Betancourt’s company currently produces
about 200,000 barrels per day — or about as much over the course of a year as
the United States uses in three days.

NABEP aims to increase its production to 500,000 barrels per day by the end of
2028, according to [recent
reports](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-10/trump-s-venezuela-
oil-venture-eyes-150-output-hike-by-late-2028).

In addition to securing a discount on 20% of NABEP’s oil, Washington also has
“first priority” to purchase all of the company’s remaining oil production for
the next 50 years, including an irrevocable right to buy its entire oil supply
in the event the U.S. declares a national emergency.

The U.S. also receives a “most favored nation” status that requires
Betancourt’s firm to disclose any other business agreements it signs, and, if
they are favorable, to grant Washington matching terms.

One person who reviewed parts of the contract was surprised at the tangible
benefits for the U.S. compared with the lack of binding commitments to
Venezuela: “I gave you 20% of my production at ‘cost plus,’ fine. I gave you
all of my production if there’s a national emergency, OK. … So what do I get
in exchange?”

A U.S. official said Rodriguez had granted NABEP 100-year oil concessions to
operate there, although this figure is not referenced in the accord and
appears to contradict Venezuelan law.

In the event of a dispute, Venezuela can’t challenge the deal in its own
courts. The agreement dictates that any conflict between the company and the
United States must be settled under U.S. law, not Venezuela’s. The two sides
even spelled out that any civil case or arbitration must be argued before the
United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas, where Trump’s
Justice Department [has turned, time and
again](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/30/us/politics/texas-judge-trump-
agenda.html), for favorable rulings.

Where U.S. law does not apply, Texas state law governs, the agreement states.

A Pentagon office has been tasked with someday executing the financial
transaction to capitalize on the U.S. government’s 35% share in the venture.
The document shows that the U.S. will pay nothing upfront but plans to acquire
its stake in Betancourt’s company by paying $0.01 per warrant share. Those
terms are set to expire on the 75th anniversary of the closing date.

In a White House statement last month, Trump touted those shares as
potentially worth “hundreds of billions,” plus dividends. But Democrats on the
Senate Armed Services Committee said they believe the Pentagon office does not
have the legal authority to execute an agreement with a foreign entity
operating in a country under U.S. sanctions.

Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson said that the Defense Department
conducts “extensive due diligence” before extending capital assistance. Wilson
declined to comment on any of the legal considerations or further technical
aspects of the deal “to protect the integrity of the process.”

Several other detailed aspects of how the company will operate are currently
under negotiation among the Trump administration, Betancourt and the parent
company, the partnership documents show. The agreement repeatedly cites a set
of “Implementation Documents” that will finalize the U.S. ownership stake and
the rights of unnamed investors.

The full force of the deal will not take effect until both parties have
complied with its closing conditions, which the agreement indicates could
happen within months.

Last month, Senate Democrats blasted what was known of the oil accord and
demanded details in a letter to Rubio, Hegseth and Secretary of Energy Chris
Wright.

“It is unclear why the American public should support this attempt to entangle
the United States with a relatively unknown foreign oil company that lacks the
capacity or credibility to develop oil fields of the magnitude described and
whose leadership has faced international criminal investigations,” four
ranking [senators said in the
letter](https://www.foreign.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/09302026%20Venezuela%20Oil%20Deal%20Rankers%20Letter_2212%201.pdf).

They asserted that most of the “oil fields are nowhere near ready for
production” and that it could “take up to a decade before global oil markets
are meaningfully impacted and the American people see any tangible benefit.”

![Two men wearing blue suits, with serious expressions, stand in front of news
microphones.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2254495662_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=1149)Secretary
of Defense Pete Hegseth, left, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio speak to
members of the media about Venezuela days after the U.S. captured President
Nicolás Maduro in January. Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images

### A Willing Partner

Almost immediately after U.S. special operations forces seized President
Nicolás Maduro in January and airlifted him out of Venezuela, Trump left
little doubt that his larger goal was to restore American access to
Venezuela’s oil reserves two decades after most U.S. firms had been ejected
from the country.

By early spring, an obscure cast of energy officials, lawyers and lobbyists
had started to craft plans to deliver on Trump’s America First energy agenda.
One person familiar with the deliberations said that U.S. officials had
considered backing an idea for publicly held American oil companies like
Chevron, Exxon and Conoco to carve up and rehabilitate Venezuela’s aging oil
sector. Another potential route went through Betancourt’s company, which is
the second largest private oil firm operating in Venezuela. Working with the
Venezuelan state company, Petróleos de Venezuela, SA, was never really an
option due to its underlying debt and history of corruption, the person said.

The option of turning to large multinational oil companies quickly stalled. In
some cases, oil executives balked at jumping back into the complexity of the
Venezuelan market; in others, firms struggled to get more than “lip service”
meetings in Washington and Caracas, according to media reports and people
familiar with the deal.

“NABEP was given priority,” one person said. “Exxon, Conoco and the others
were treated as second class.”

Betancourt’s star was rising in the Trump administration. He had served as an
interlocutor for Washington with the Maduro government and had ties to some
leaders of the Venezuelan opposition, according to current and former U.S.
officials. He had also provided information that helped the U.S. forces seize
Venezuelan oil tankers and that aided strategy and planning before the capture
of Maduro, [Reuters
reported](https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/venezuelan-billionaire-us-
investigated-money-laundering-now-has-pentagon-oil-2026-09-05/).

In addition, Betancourt had developed a good relationship with Rodríguez, whom
Trump had backed as the country’s interim president. And Betancourt had done
so despite the fact that her influential brother, National Assembly President
Jorge Rodríguez, had [accused him of
corruption](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9EKU6sn7_-U&pp=ygUySm9yZ2UgUm9kcmlndWV6IGRlbnVuY2lhIGFsZWphbmRybyBiZXRhbmNvdXJ0IDIwMjA%3D)
in a televised speech in 2020, according to former U.S. officials and press
reports.

U.S. officials also saw practical reasons to partner with Betancourt, several
people said. He and his then-business partner in the U.S., Harry Sargeant, a
Trump supporter, appeared to be a rare success story in a battered industry,
operating some of the only active oil fields in the country.  

“The main thing I found promising is that the fields are producing in
Venezuela,” said a former State Department official who analyzed the company’s
activities. “I think it’s particularly important that you buy into fields that
are producing. … If your policy goal is to raise production quickly, this
makes sense.”  

But partnering with Betancourt posed major challenges.

For starters, the 46-year-old billionaire was confined to house arrest on his
[300-acre Oxfordshire
estate](https://www.dailymail.com/news/article-15348503/Billionaire-wanted-
Switzerland-money-laundering.html) in England, fighting off a Swiss
extradition request tied to an international money-laundering probe.
Betancourt could fly to his [$46 million London
residence](https://www.dailymail.com/news/article-15348503/Billionaire-wanted-
Switzerland-money-laundering.html) by private helicopter — but his [Venezuelan
and Italian passports](https://www.thetimes.com/world/latin-
america/article/venezuelan-oil-man-investigated-overseas-is-key-broker-for-
trump-pv0kbjt6m) were locked down, and British authorities had barred him from
driving on public roads, according to media reports about the special bail
arrangement.

Betancourt’s legal problems stemmed from his role in troubled Venezuelan
energy projects during the corrupt rule of former President Hugo Chávez.
Several of Betancourt’s known or alleged associates were charged or convicted
in a major U.S. money-laundering investigation known as Operation Money
Flight. Betancourt surfaced as a suspect in the U.S. case and is still under
investigation for suspected money laundering by [authorities in
Spain](https://english.elpais.com/international/2026-09-14/united-states-
stalls-spanish-investigation-into-alejandro-betancourt-its-new-oil-czar-in-
venezuela.html), according to former U.S. and European officials and [press
reports](https://www.occrp.org/en/project/openlux/jet-setting-venezuelan-
businessman-in-corruption-probe-linked-to-luxembourg-firms).

The most popular leader of the Venezuelan opposition in exile, María Corina
Machado, recently described Betancourt as having been involved in “obscene
corruption” that caused great suffering for the Venezuelan people, according
to [a recent New York Times
interview](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/world/americas/venezuela-
machado-trump-oil-deal.html?eafs_enabled=false).

Betancourt has not been charged in any country. His lawyer has maintained his
client’s innocence, saying Betancourt has been unfairly maligned because
people associate him with a group of wealthy young Venezuelans, some of whom
have been accused of wrongdoing, according to [press
reports](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cyvze0n4vy1o).

Many Venezuelans see Betancourt as a “totemic, emblematic, corrupt figure,”
said Brian Naranjo, a former senior U.S. diplomat in Venezuela, in an
interview.

“He is not really an oil man,” Naranjo said. “The talent he brings is that
he’s a new person in a long line of Venezuelan businesspeople who deal in
influence. Their big lever is connections and influence. It is know-who, not
know-how.”

In a [recent interview](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-
spokesman/2026/09/secretary-of-state-marco-rubio-with-sergio-novelli-on-al-
dia-con-sergio-novelli) with Spanish language media, Rubio defended
Betancourt, praising his oil company’s work in Venezuela and his support for
factions of the Venezuelan opposition in exile.

Rubio downplayed the legal scrutiny Betancourt has faced, saying a review
conducted with U.S. law enforcement agencies indicated “there were no
investigations of him in our system.”

> “The talent he brings is that he’s a new person in a long line of Venezuelan
> businesspeople who deal in influence. … It is know-who, not know-how.”
>
> Brian Naranjo, former U.S. diplomat

It remains unclear exactly how Betancourt shed the travel restrictions imposed
by European authorities. But [The Washington Post
reported](https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2026/08/27/us-intervened-
criminal-probe-venezuelan-oilman-alejandro-betancourt/) that senior Trump
administration officials, including Deputy Secretary of State Christopher
Landau, former Attorney General Pam Bondi and then-Deputy Attorney General
Todd Blanche, petitioned their foreign counterparts to allow Betancourt to
travel freely and to close their investigations into him and his business
ventures.

The Trump administration’s next hurdle to working with Betancourt was figuring
out how to legally invest. The government’s $200 billion investment agency,
the International Development Finance Corporation, was created to do just that
but is currently barred by U.S. law from operating in Venezuela.

At different points through the summer, aides to Office of Management and
Budget Director Russell Vought stepped in, pressing Defense and State
department officials to consider alternate financing paths, according to one
person familiar with the deal’s progression.

By July, the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital, headed by David Lorch,
emerged as a potential solution.

Lorch, who had moved to the Pentagon from Deputy Defense Secretary Steve
Feinberg’s private equity firm, Cerberus Capital, quickly embraced the idea,
according to people familiar with the deal. Lorch and other Pentagon and State
Department officials flew to Caracas in the final days of that month and
agreed in principle to a deal. The details would be hammered out back in
Washington, the people said.

A Pentagon spokesperson said Lorch declined to comment.

On Aug. 5, Betancourt strode into a conference room behind the art deco facade
of the old Greyhound Bus Terminal in downtown Washington that houses an
auxiliary Pentagon office. The assembled Defense Department officials gave the
Venezuelan billionaire the red carpet treatment, lining up to shake his hand,
according to people familiar with the meeting. But some in the room were
stunned to discover that the U.S. government was preparing to do business with
Betancourt, the people familiar with the meeting said.

Betancourt was accompanied by Jacob Hirshman, the chief executive and co-
founder of Erebor Bank, the first new bank chartered after Trump returned to
office, according to people familiar with the meeting. The bank, backed by
Trump supporters and investors Peter Thiel and Palmer Luckey, has vowed to
reconnect Venezuela to the world economy.

Hirshman did not respond to a request for comment.

Lorch told the group, which included dozens of former Wall Street associates
he’d hired into the office, that the alliance with Betancourt was a major
“opportunity” to fulfill one of the Trump administration’s top goals, securing
benefits to the United States and Venezuela for decades to come.

The meeting touched off a month of around-the-clock calls and video
conferences.  
  
People familiar with the deal’s progression said Lorch soon became involved in
structuring key aspects of the deal beyond its financing, including how the
board would sit for 15 years and choose its successors. One said he put an
explicit premium on setting up the venture in a way that it could not be
undone by Trump’s successor.  
  
The months of work on the deal burst into public view on Aug. 28 with a Trump
announcement on Truth Social.

“The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the
Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” Trump posted
on a Friday night.

Two days later, Hegseth, Rubio, Betancourt and Alvarado signed the deal.

The post [The Secret Terms of Trump’s Venezuelan Oil
Deal](https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-venezuela-oil-agreement-terms)
appeared first on [ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
